payload.instructions: Preserve all candidate IDs and distinctions. Broader parent themes organize evidence; they do not imply measurement equivalence.

themes.disagreements: contradictions, weak signals, and proxy distinctions
evidence_ids: at most 12 representative supplied modeling evidence IDs
themes.interpretation: common or complementary evidence
themes.name: theme

themes.disagreements: Lesion size (183) and mass localization (166) exhibit dual roles as confounders and effect modifiers; proliferative markers (196, 197) and dissection procedure (201) are primarily effect modifiers, while others (182, 193, 195, 198, 199, 200, 202) show negligible signals.
themes.interpretation: Tumor morphological and nodal assessments ranging from negligible prognostic signals to robust dual roles in confounding and treatment heterogeneity.
themes.name: Tumor Morphological and Nodal Assessment

themes.disagreements: PET metrics (164, 168) and lobectomy type (190) demonstrate dual roles as confounders and effect modifiers; orbital/cranial findings (173) and leptomeningeal enhancement (181) are primarily effect modifiers, while others remain purely prognostic.
themes.interpretation: Advanced radiographic imaging findings showing a spectrum from purely prognostic importance to strong treatment heterogeneity and confounding.
themes.name: Advanced Radiographic Imaging

themes.disagreements: High consistency across Ki67, KEAP1, and KRAS VAF, all showing strong signals for effect modification and outcome prognosis.
themes.interpretation: Molecular and proliferative biomarkers acting as consistent indicators of treatment effect modification.
themes.name: Molecular and Pathological Biomarkers

themes.disagreements: Line of therapy (184) and calcium carbonate (203) show dual roles; cisplatin (204), denosumab (205), and G12C inhibitors (207) are primarily effect modifiers; lisinopril (209) is a clear confounder.
themes.interpretation: Pharmacotherapy agents with divergent roles ranging from simple confounding to complex effect modification and prognosis.
themes.name: Pharmacotherapy and Systemic Treatment

themes.disagreements: Pulmonary diagnosis (194), liver metastasis (188), and baseline health markers (170) show dual roles; illicit drug use (162) is primarily a confounder, while general liver function (187) and auscultation (191) are negligible or prognostic.
themes.interpretation: Comorbidities and organ-specific health markers showing varying levels of confounding and treatment heterogeneity.
themes.name: Organ Function and Comorbidities

themes.disagreements: Knee osteoarthritis (177) is a dominant confounder, whereas other clinical assessments (174, 180) provide only weak or purely prognostic signals.
themes.interpretation: General clinical and laboratory metrics where confounding is limited to specific markers.
themes.name: Clinical and Laboratory Metrics

themes.disagreements: Morphine (217) demonstrates dual roles; living arrangements (189) act as a confounder, while oxycodone (211) remains purely prognostic.
themes.interpretation: Social context and pain management markers with divergent roles in treatment prediction and effect modification.
themes.name: Social and Pain Management

themes.disagreements: Prior immunotherapy (169) demonstrates dual roles as a confounder and effect modifier, while imaging procedures (163) are primarily effect modifiers.
themes.interpretation: Procedural and therapy history markers providing evidence for treatment heterogeneity and confounding.
themes.name: Procedural and Therapy History

themes.disagreements: Pemetrexed (212) exhibits both confounding and modification signals, while MET amplification (214, 219), PD-L1/p40 (243, 248), and PI3K (254) are predominantly effect modifiers.
themes.interpretation: Molecular and intracellular signaling biomarkers providing evidence for treatment heterogeneity.
themes.name: Molecular and Signaling Biomarkers

themes.disagreements: Metastasis location (216) and optic chiasm enhancement (235) show dual roles as confounders and modifiers, whereas meningeal thickening (213) and posterior fossa features (261, 262) are more strongly prognostic.
themes.interpretation: Radiological and structural characteristics of the brain and primary tumor assessing prognosis and treatment interaction.
themes.name: Neuro-Radiological and Structural Imaging

themes.disagreements: Bone density (239, 240) and respiratory status (241, 242) are high-confidence confounders; systemic health markers (259, 260) show modest effect modification signals in causal forests.
themes.interpretation: Markers of organ-level dysfunction and general comorbidities that primarily drive treatment assignment and outcome prognosis.
themes.name: Systemic Health and Comorbidities

themes.disagreements: Metabolic response (215) and NYHA class (231) are credible effect modifiers, while pain severity (245), mucositis (220), and organomegaly (238) are primarily prognostic.
themes.interpretation: Functional and symptomatic indicators of patient status reflecting either treatment heterogeneity or outcome prognosis.
themes.name: Clinical Performance and Symptomatology

themes.disagreements: Systemic inflammation (228) and N-stage (230) show robust evidence for dual roles (confounder and modifier), whereas Napsin A (224) is primarily a modifier.
themes.interpretation: Inflammatory and pathological markers demonstrating strong influence on both prognosis and treatment effect.
themes.name: Inflammation and Pathology

themes.disagreements: Palliative care status (246) is a very strong prognostic factor, while other operational and demographic features (232, 233, 234, 237) show weak or inconsistent signals.
themes.interpretation: Care preferences and demographic factors that primarily serve as markers for severity of illness and treatment selection.
themes.name: Care Preferences and Operational Factors

themes.disagreements: Radiation therapy (263) shows weaker univariable signals than platinum chemotherapy (267, 268); radiation session count (281) predicts treatment while radiosurgery history (282) is primarily prognostic.
themes.interpretation: Prior oncology and radiation treatments act as both confounders and effect modifiers, though signal strength varies by modality.
themes.name: Oncology and Radiation Treatment History

themes.disagreements: Extremely strong univariable signals for treatment and outcome in symptoms (269, 270) and PROs (278, 279) potentially mask more nuanced effect modification captured by causal forests.
themes.interpretation: Symptomatic burden and functional PROs are powerful predictors of treatment assignment and outcome prognosis, with evidence for effect modification.
themes.name: Patient-Reported Burden and Function

themes.disagreements: Respiratory rate (287) is a strong confounder; renal function (286) primarily predicts treatment; creatinine (299) and albumin (295) dominate treatment prediction while calcium (297) predicts outcome; sodium (301) is weak.
themes.interpretation: Systemic vitals and serum chemistry exhibit high utility for treatment prediction (confounding) and evidence for effect modification.
themes.name: Systemic Vitals and Serum Chemistry

themes.disagreements: Treatment prediction is consistent across pulmonary imaging (273, 276) and molecular markers (289), but evidence for treatment-heterogeneity varies in strength and fold consistency.
themes.interpretation: Thoracic diagnostics and radiological markers frequently predict treatment (potential instruments) and show moderate evidence for effect modification.
themes.name: Thoracic and Molecular Diagnostics

themes.disagreements: The group ranges from clear confounders (PPI 271) and modifiers (Psychiatric 272) to imaging features (304, 309, 310) which strongly predict outcome and effect heterogeneity.
themes.interpretation: Medical/neurological history and cranial neuroimaging provide heterogeneous evidence for both confounding and treatment-effect modification.
themes.name: Neuro-Medical History and Cranial Imaging

themes.disagreements: ROS1 status (291) is a strong treatment predictor and modifier, whereas rearrangement status (292) is weak; surgical status (311, 312, 314) consistently shows effect modification.
themes.interpretation: Genetic markers and surgical/pathological outcomes demonstrate evidence for effect modification, with varying strength across specific markers.
themes.name: Genetic and Surgical Pathological Status

system:
You review pretreatment candidate measurements using modeling evidence
from one outer-training fold. First identify themes across candidates; then
reconcile their roles as confounder, effect_modifier, both, or neither.
All evidence is fallible. No individual family, p-value, or support frequency is
a hard selection gate. A credible complementary signal can justify retention
even when other methods shrink it away. Do not mistake correlated aliases or
proxies for multiple independent discoveries. Themes organize evidence; they
do not establish equivalence, merge measurements, or transfer a role to every
theme member. Preserve investigator-locked roles exactly.

Treatment prediction, outcome prognosis, and confounding are distinct. Discuss
whether a candidate could be a common cause rather than an instrument or only a
prognostic factor. Effect modification needs treatment-heterogeneity evidence;
outcome main-effect importance alone does not establish it. Univariable logistic
interactions are on the log-odds scale and unadjusted for other covariates.
Orthogonal linear models, candidate R-learners, and causal forests assess the
probability/outcome scale after elastic-net nuisance adjustment. Their targets
and biases differ. A model family is evidence, not an independent replication.

Use exposure and evaluability denominators. Missing or nonconverged fits are not
negative votes. Repeated samples and folds overlap; support fractions are not
causal probabilities or formal stability-selection error guarantees. Raw and BH
p-values do not correct the upstream adaptive discovery process. Permutation
importance can be diluted by correlated alternatives and does not prove a
causal role. Compare fold consistency, methods, subsets, and conflicting facts.
Definitions and theme names cannot establish a role without the supplied
empirical evidence. Never invent an oracle, data-generating process, or hidden
truth. Return the requested JSON and cite only supplied evidence IDs.
